analysis.notes: A tour of secondary dominants. E7 is V7/vi but resolves deceptively to A7 (V7/ii) instead of Am; that A7 then resolves to Dm7. In the bridge the same E7 does land on Am7, and D7 (V7/V) sets up Dm7–G7. The last eight bars contain the classic IV–iv move (Fmaj7 to Fm6) before a iii–VI–ii–V–I run home. Two bars per chord makes it a great tune for practising rhythmic comping variety.

learning.why: Slow harmonic rhythm and a chain of secondary dominants: perfect for learning to hear V7/x chords and to comp with variety when a chord lasts two bars.
drills: Comp two bars per chord using a different rhythm in the second bar than the first.
Over each dominant, play the 3rd on beat one and resolve it by half step into the next chord.
Solo with the mixolydian scale on each dominant, targeting the 3rd.
Loop the last eight bars and practise the Fmaj7–Fm6 colour change.
listen: Django Reinhardt with the Quintette du Hot Club de France
milestones: Know the form and changes from memory
Comp shells through the form without looking
Comp drop-2 voicings with the trio
Play a chord-tone solo over the whole form
Play the melody from memory (learn it by ear from a recording)
